newsitem.title: SPAIN: Spain court orders "dirty war" files opened.
newsitem.headline: Spain court orders "dirty war" files opened.

text.p: Spain's Supreme Court ordered the government on Saturday to open secret files which could implicate former prime minister Felipe Gonzalez in the 1980s "dirty war" against Basque guerrillas.

After four days of deliberations, 33 magistrates overturned a decision last August by the conservative Popular Party (PP) government to keep the documents classified for reasons of state security. The government said it would abide by the order.
"The government complies with the Supreme Court decision and will act in accordance," government spokesman Miguel Angel Rodriguez told reporters.

Though Supreme Court justices probing the death squads have decided against questioning Gonzalez so far, the "dirty war" scandal tainted his Socialists and contributed to their election defeat in March 1996 after 13 years in power.

The secret CESID papers, named after Spain's military intelligence agency where they originated, purportedly show Gonzalez and associates set up "anti-terrorist" squads to combat separatist guerrilla group ETA (Basque Homeland and Freedom).
In the early 1980s, ETA was killing about one person a week and the government was under pressure to respond. ETA has killed some 800 people in a 29-year struggle for Basque independence.
Lower courts investigating the campaign of kidnappings, torture and killings say the documents contain vital information needed to prosecute former senior officials and security chiefs.

Spain's Defence Minister Eduardo Serra had warned against declassifying the documents. But a ministry spokesman said on Saturday he did not think Spain's allies would lose confidence in the government's ability to maintain official secrets.
"This decision has not made the Spanish secret services lose credibility," the spokesman said.
The Supreme Court ordered the opening of 13 of 18 classified documents sought by three lower courts.

Judges and officials have said those documents could provide evidence to reopen investigations into whether Gonzalez and his associates oversaw death squads that killed 28 people from 1983-1987. One third of the victims were targeted by mistake.
Several former Socialist officials and security chiefs have already been charged in the "dirty war" scandal.

Last month, the court asked the government to hand over the documents so it could decide whether to declassify them. The government authorised a temporary transfer and judges then studied the originals on microfilm for the first time.
The secret files have dogged the Socialists since 1995, when the daily El Mundo started publishing, bit by bit, copies of the documents allegedly stolen by a former spy.
But their authenticity was questionable.
The documents first came to light in a complicated intrigue which ex-officials on trial for the "dirty war" have said was a conspiracy of aggrieved rivals, judges and journalists.

The copies were found during a court search of the prison cell of ex-spy Juan Alberto Perote, who claimed to have stolen them from CESID. Judges said he tried to swallow some of them during the search.
Perote was sacked by CESID but left only after stuffing a briefcase full of incriminating documents which he peddled to buyers with grudges against the Socialists.
Most political parties praised the court decision.

Basque Nationalist Party spokesman Inaki Anasagasti said it restored his confidence in the judicial system. He praised the court for rejecting the government's argument that declassifying the papers could endanger state security.
"The only thing put in danger is whoever committed or permitted some type of crime," he said.
The Socialists said there was nothing in the documents that should cause concern among citizens of Spain.
